claims.text: The baseline alloy is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Casting and homogenization can produce a single solid-solution state in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed modified alloy is CoCrFeNiTi0.8Nb0.2, corresponding to Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Ti16Nb4 in atomic percent.
The proposed modification substitutes approximately 10 at.% of Ti with Nb.
The Nb-modified alloy can retain the same single solid-solution phase as the baseline alloy.
Atomic-size mismatch among the constituent elements provides a measure of lattice distortion.
The constituent elements of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi have similar atomic radii and therefore produce minimal lattice distortion.
Minimal lattice distortion permits relatively unimpeded dislocation glide in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Relatively unimpeded dislocation glide causes favorable plasticity but low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Nb atoms are larger than the atoms they replace and consequently increase lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi0.8Nb0.2.
Increased lattice distortion from Nb substitution raises barriers to dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
Nb-induced solid-solution strengthening will increase hardness and yield strength while reducing ductility.
The single-phase Nb-modified alloy will have higher hardness and yield or compressive strength than the baseline at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
The Nb-modified alloy will exhibit lower plastic strain than the baseline at both test temperatures.
The reduction in plastic strain caused by Nb substitution will be especially pronounced at 600 °C.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has superior plasticity and machinability relative to the proposed Nb-modified variant.
Nb addition may trigger secondary-phase formation that obscures the isolated effect of lattice distortion.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase baseline and Nb-modified alloys tested from 25 °C through 600 °C under elastic-plastic loading.

contradictions.description: The phrase 'substitute approximately 10 at.% of Ti with Nb' is inconsistent with CoCrFeNiTi0.8Nb0.2. That formula replaces 20% of the original Ti-site amount and yields 4 at.% Nb overall; replacing 10% of Ti would instead correspond to approximately CoCrFeNiTi0.9Nb0.1.

The boundary restricts the hypothesis to verified single-phase alloys, and the uncertainty field says secondary phases would obscure isolation of lattice distortion, but the falsification rule treats detection of secondary phases as falsifying the mechanism. Secondary phases would ordinarily make the intended controlled comparison invalid or confounded rather than directly refute a mechanism explicitly limited to single-phase material.
